resps:
The simple clause *“A gymnast is in the air, performing a stunt.”* may look modest, but it compresses an entire universe of physics, artistry, and human determination into a single breath. Let us unpack it, layer by layer, until the *moment of flight* becomes as vivid as if we were watching it live.

First, consider the subject: *a gymnast*. This is not merely “someone who flips.” A gymnast is a *fusion of athlete and artist*, someone who has spent thousands of hours conditioning muscles that most people never consciously activate. The *gymnast’s body* is a living archive of micro-injuries healed, calluses smoothed, and fears overwritten by muscle memory. When we say “a gymnast,” we invoke a person whose daily life is measured in tenths of a point and whose dreams are scored by judges holding tablets instead of clipboards.

Next, the phrase *“is in the air”* catapults us from the horizontal world of mats and beams into the vertical dimension of *weightlessness*. This is not the gentle floating of a leaf; it is a *violent negotiation with gravity* that lasts perhaps 1.2 seconds yet feels like an eternity to the performer. During that sliver of time, the gymnast’s inner ear is screaming for orientation while the eyes—trained to spot a fixed point on the horizon—are searching for the *visual anchor* that will tell the body when to untuck, when to extend, when to prepare for landing. The air itself becomes a *tangible medium*, thick with chalk dust and the faint smell of resin, pushing back against the athlete’s limbs like an invisible coach.

Then comes the participial phrase *“performing a stunt.”* The word *stunt* is deceptively casual; in gymnastics it is a euphemism for a *calculated risk*. It might be a double-twisting double back somersault, a skill so demanding that only a few dozen humans on the planet can execute it with consistent success. Each twist is a *miniature hurricane* of torque generated by the hips and shoulders, timed so precisely that a millisecond’s delay will turn triumph into trauma. The stunt is also a *narrative arc* compressed into two heartbeats: takeoff (rising action), peak (climax), and landing (resolution). Spectators see only the arc; the gymnast feels every chapter.

Embedded in the stunt is the *silent dialogue between athlete and apparatus*. Even though the apparatus is absent from the sentence, it is present in the *muscle memory* of the gymnast’s calves, which remember the spring of the tumbling track, and in the *phantom sensation* of the bar still tingling in the palms. The air itself becomes a *substitute apparatus*, a partner that offers no grip yet demands perfect form. The gymnast must *recreate the stability of the floor* in a place where nothing is solid.

We must also consider the *psychological altitude* of the moment. While the body is 12 feet off the ground, the mind is navigating a *mental lattice* of checkpoints: “Tight core, chin tucked, knees together, spot the landing, prepare for the roll-out if the rebound is off.” Each checkpoint is a *microscopic prayer* whispered in the language of proprioception. The gymnast’s brain is running a *Monte Carlo simulation* of every possible outcome, discarding the catastrophic ones in nanoseconds.

Finally, the sentence ends, but the *echo of the landing* reverberates forward in time. Long after the chalk has settled, the stunt lives on in *slow-motion replays*, in judges’ notations, and in the *collective gasp* of an audience that momentarily forgot to breathe. The gymnast will replay the flight in dreams, sometimes feeling the *perfect stick*, sometimes jolting awake with the sensation of a wobble that never actually happened. In this way, the stunt is not confined to the air; it *haunts the ground* as well, shaping the next day’s training, the next risk, the next leap into the unknown.

Thus, the eight-word sentence is a *capsule biography* of discipline, danger, and transcendence, a reminder that what looks like a fleeting trick is, in reality, a *lifetime condensed into 1.2 seconds of flight*.

doc.prompt: Write a rubric for rating how good a teenager's essay is. Give your final summary, following 6 asterisk symbols (******).

arg_0: [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a rubric for rating how good a teenager's essay is. Give your final summary, following 6 asterisk symbols (******).", "type": "text"}]

resps:
Teen Essay Rubric (100 points total)

1. Focus & Thesis (15 pts)
   • 15 – Clear, arguable, and specific thesis that guides every paragraph.  
   • 12 – Thesis is present and mostly clear; occasional drift.  
   • 9 – Thesis is vague or shifts; reader must infer main claim.  
   • 6 – Thesis missing or contradictory; essay wanders.  
   • 3 – No discernible central idea.

2. Content & Evidence (20 pts)
   • 20 – Relevant, well-explained evidence from credible sources or personal insight; shows original thinking.  
   • 16 – Good evidence, generally explained; minor gaps.  
   • 12 – Adequate evidence, but some is weak or under-explained.  
   • 8 – Limited or repetitive evidence; little explanation.  
   • 4 – Unsupported generalizations or factual errors.

3. Organization & Flow (15 pts)
   • 15 – Logical progression; strong transitions; intro, body, conclusion work seamlessly.  
   • 12 – Mostly logical; transitions present but occasionally mechanical.  
   • 9 – Some lapses in order; abrupt shifts.  
   • 6 – Disorganized; hard to follow.  
   • 3 – No clear structure.

4. Voice & Style (15 pts)
   • 15 – Engaging, authentic teen voice; varied sentence patterns; tone fits purpose.  
   • 12 – Generally lively; some sentence variety; minor lapses in tone.  
   • 9 – Flat or inconsistent voice; repetitive structure.  
   • 6 – Awkward or inappropriate tone; little variety.  
   • 3 – Monotonous or confusing style.

5. Language & Mechanics (15 pts)
   • 15 – Virtually error-free; word choice precise; grammar, spelling, punctuation enhance clarity.  
   • 12 – Few minor errors; meaning never impaired.  
   • 9 – Several noticeable errors; occasional distraction.  
   • 6 – Frequent errors that interfere with understanding.  
   • 3 – Persistent errors obscure meaning.

6. Insight & Reflection (20 pts)
   • 20 – Demonstrates deep reflection; connects topic to broader issues or personal growth; shows critical thinking.  
   • 16 – Solid reflection; some connections made.  
   • 12 – Surface-level reflection; predictable observations.  
   • 8 – Little reflection; mostly summary.  
   • 4 – No reflection; purely descriptive.

Grade Bands
A 90–100 | B 80–89 | C 70–79 | D 60–69 | F <60

******
Use this rubric to give teens transparent, balanced feedback: celebrate what’s working, pinpoint next steps, and keep the door open for revision.

<<A Royal Mandate Most Solemn: A Letter Penn’d in the Quill of Master William Shakespeare>>

---

**To the Noble and Right Worshipful Lords, Knights, and Commons of this Realm,**  
**From the Hand of a Loyal Subject, who writes by the King’s express command.**

---

Most potent, grave, and reverend signiors,  
Whose hearts do beat with loyalty as true as steel,  
Give ear unto this scroll, wherein is writ  
The sovereign will of him whose word is law,  
Whose breath doth stir the winds and calm the seas,  
Our dread liege lord, King **Henricus Quintus**,  
Whose crown is circled round with stars of right,  
And whose decree doth thunder from the throne.

---

### I. **Of the King’s Mandate Touching the Realm’s Defence**

> “Let no man sleep whilst England’s watch is kept.”

By royal seal and signet, thus it stands:  
That every shire shall furnish forth its men,  
In number full, in spirit resolute,  
To man the walls from Berwick to the Solent.  
Let smiths beat ploughshares into blades once more,  
And let the drum be heard in every vale.  
The King commands that none shall shirk this call,  
Lest treason’s brand be set upon his brow.

---

### II. **Of the King’s Instruction Touching the Coin and Crown**

> “No purse shall be unopened to the realm.”

Let every lord and guild and merchant true  
Render unto the Exchequer what is due.  
A tithe of ten in every hundred marks  
Shall be collected ere the harvest moon.  
Let not the cry of “privilege” be raised—  
The King hath need, and need brooks no delay.  
Whoso withholds shall answer to the law,  
And find his lands escheat unto the Crown.

---

### III. **Of the King’s Pleasure Touching the Clergy and the Word**

> “Let pulpits ring with loyalty, not schism.”

The bishops four and twenty are enjoined  
To preach obedience, not Rome’s command.  
Let no priest whisper foreign sovereignty,  
Nor sow the seeds of discord in the flock.  
The King is head of Church as well as State—  
This truth shall be inscribed in every heart,  
And taught to babes e’en at their mothers’ knees.

---

### IV. **Of the King’s Mercy and His Wrath**

> “The lion may roar, yet spare the lamb that kneels.”

To those who yield, the King extends his grace—  
A pardon sealed in wax and signed in blood.  
But to the proud, the plotter, and the false,  
The axe shall fall as swift as winter’s frost.  
Let none mistake his mercy for weakness,  
Nor think his wrath a thing of empty sound.  
The King hath eyes in every shadowed hall,  
And ears in every whispered corridor.

---

### V. **Of the Bearer of This Letter**

> “He who bears this scroll is arm’d with sovereign voice.”

Know ye that I, **Gideon of Ely**,  
Do speak not as myself, but as the King.  
My words are not my own, but his decree.  
Dispute me not, lest ye dispute the Crown.  
I ride with seal and sword, and none may bar  
My passage through the gates of any town.  
Let all who read this letter bend the knee,  
And swear anew their fealty to the throne.

---

Thus ends the royal mandate, writ in haste,  
Yet sealed with solemn oath and sacred trust.  
Let it be nailed to every churchyard door,  
And cried aloud in every market square.  
For so commands the King, whose will is fate,  
Whose voice is thunder, and whose law is love.

> *“God save the King, and keep his realm in peace.”*

---

**Given under my hand this 14th day of July,**  
**In the year of our Lord 1599,**  
**At the Palace of Whitehall, in the shadow of the Crown.**

**Your obedient servant,**  
**Gideon of Ely**  
*Clerk of the Royal Chamber, and Messenger of the King’s Word*

resps:
"common signs and symptoms of abdominal and pelvic dissemination of ovarian cancer arise from the spread of malignant cells onto the peritoneal surfaces, omentum, bowel serosa, mesentery, diaphragm, and pelvic organs. these manifestations evolve gradually, often masquerading as benign gastrointestinal or genitourinary complaints, which contributes to delayed diagnosis. the most frequent early clue is a vague, poorly localized discomfort or pressure felt deep in the lower abdomen or pelvis. patients describe it as a dull ache, heaviness, or sense of fullness that persists for weeks and is not clearly related to meals, menses, or physical activity. as tumor nodules coat the peritoneum, they irritate nerve endings and produce this chronic discomfort that gradually intensifies.

progressive abdominal distention is another hallmark. it is multifactorial: accumulation of malignant ascites, bulky omental caking, and enlarged lymph nodes all contribute. the patient notices that skirts, pants, or belts become tight within a short period despite stable body weight. the abdomen may take on a rounded, tense appearance, sometimes with visible superficial venous distention. shifting dullness and a fluid wave can often be elicited on physical examination. the ascitic fluid itself can be under tension, causing additional pressure symptoms such as early satiety, nausea, and heartburn. patients report that they feel full after only a few bites of food, a symptom termed “suprapubic fullness” or “appetite shutdown.” this early satiety is compounded when tumor plaques coat the stomach and small bowel serosa, impairing normal peristalsis and creating a functional ileus.

bowel habit changes are common. partial obstruction from serosal implants leads to colicky pain, bloating, and intermittent constipation alternating with loose stools. if the sigmoid colon or rectosigmoid is encased, tenesmus and narrow caliber stools may appear. conversely, involvement of the ileocecal region can precipitate diarrhea or steatorrhea due to lymphatic obstruction. when carcinomatosis advances, complete bowel obstruction supervenes, heralded by obstipation, copious bilious vomiting, and tympanic abdominal distention; this is an oncologic emergency.

urinary symptoms reflect either direct bladder serosal involvement or external compression by tumor masses and ascites. patients experience urinary frequency, urgency, and nocturia because the bladder cannot expand fully. dysuria may occur if tumor infiltrates the trigone or urethra. hydronephrosis develops when malignant nodes encase the ureters, leading to flank pain, hematuria, and eventually renal insufficiency. bilateral ureteral obstruction is a late but grave complication.

pelvic dissemination often produces deep dyspareunia and a sensation of pelvic heaviness or “something falling out.” on bimanual examination, the cul-de-sac feels obliterated, and nodularity along the uterosacral ligaments is palpable. rectovaginal examination may reveal a firm, fixed shelf of tumor in the pouch of douglas. as the disease spreads to the parametria and lateral pelvic sidewalls, sciatic-type pain radiating down the posterior thigh may appear due to nerve root involvement.

systemic manifestations include unintentional weight loss, fatigue, and progressive cachexia. the metabolic demands of widespread tumor, combined with reduced oral intake and malabsorption from peritoneal carcinomatosis, lead to muscle wasting and hypoalbuminemia. patients often notice that their face looks gaunt while the abdomen continues to enlarge, creating a stark contrast. anemia of chronic disease contributes to pallor, dyspnea on exertion, and palpitations. thrombocytosis and hypercoagulability predispose to deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, so unilateral leg swelling or sudden pleuritic chest pain may be the first clue to disseminated disease.

respiratory compromise occurs when ascitic fluid tracks through diaphragmatic defects into the pleural space, producing malignant pleural effusions. patients report progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, and a dry cough. physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at one or both lung bases. imaging shows layering fluid with or without pleural nodularity. diaphragmatic irritation can also cause referred pain to the shoulder tip via the phrenic nerve.

lymphedema of the lower extremities develops when bulky pelvic and para-aortic nodes obstruct lymphatic return. the patient notices tightness in the thighs or calves, followed by pitting edema that becomes non-pitting over time. skin changes such as peau d’orange and recurrent cellulitis may ensue.

less common but notable signs include umbilical metastasis (sister mary joseph node) presenting as a hard, fixed nodule within or near the umbilicus that may ulcerate or bleed. subcutaneous peritoneal seedlings along laparoscopy or surgical scars produce painful, firm nodules. malignant ascites can also track into the abdominal wall, causing diffuse induration.

psychosocial symptoms should not be overlooked. chronic pain, sleep disruption, and the visible distortion of body image from ascites and cachexia lead to anxiety, depression, and social withdrawal. patients often express frustration at the prolonged diagnostic odyssey and the vague nature of their complaints.

in summary, abdominal and pelvic dissemination of ovarian cancer manifests through a constellation of progressive, nonspecific, yet relentlessly advancing symptoms. persistent abdominal or pelvic discomfort, increasing girth from ascites, early satiety, bowel and urinary changes, deep dyspareunia, and systemic decline form the core clinical picture. heightened awareness of this pattern, especially in postmenopausal women or those with hereditary risk, is essential for timely recognition and intervention."

resps:
Imagine your bike is a friendly horse that wants to stay upright.  
First, put on your helmet so your head stays safe.

1. Get on: Stand beside the bike, squeeze the brakes so it doesn’t roll, then swing one leg over and sit on the seat. Both feet should touch the ground.

2. Look ahead: Pick a tree or a mailbox far in front of you and keep your eyes on it. Your bike follows where you look.

3. Push and glide: Push off with both feet and let the bike glide. Try to keep your feet off the ground for a few seconds. Feel how the bike balances when it moves.

4. Add pedals: When gliding feels easy, rest your feet on the pedals. Push one pedal down, then the other, in a smooth circle. Keep your eyes on that tree.

5. Steer gently: If you want to turn right, press the right handlebar just a little. The bike leans and turns. Do the same on the left for the other way.

6. Stop safely: When you want to stop, squeeze both brakes evenly. Put one foot down so you don’t tip over.

Practice a few glides and pedal rides each day. Soon the bike will feel as steady as your own two feet.

**[Verge of the Weird—Renaissance Rap]**  
*(Beat: lute strings plucked over 808s, a harpsichord arpeggio that keeps glitching)*  

---

**[Verse 1: The Medici Mirror-Maze]**  
Yo, I’m **Cosimo in a hall of smoke and mirrors**,  
Every reflection’s a ledger—debt gets clearer.  
I flip a florin, it lands on *esoterica*,  
Now my banker’s face is a Botticelli replica.  
Gold leaf on the ceiling, mold grief on the floor,  
I hire monks to audit the void at the core.  
They chant in Fibonacci, incense in fractals,  
While I hedge my soul on a plague-insured vassal.  

---

**[Hook: Da Vinci’s Drone Cam]**  
*Skrrt—Leonardo’s bird-machine got Wi-Fi,*  
Streaming aerial shots of your third eye.  
He sketched a tank, then a tank of consciousness,  
Left a voicemail: “Perspective is monstrous.”  
**[Auto-tuned ghost of Machiavelli ad-libs]**  
“Princes in the chat—type ‘amoral’ if you feel me!”  

---

**[Verse 2: The Printing Press Possession]**  
Gutenberg’s press got a poltergeist—  
Every page it spits is a papercut slice of Christ.  
I’m **Erasmus in the margins, annotating in tongues**,  
While Luther nails a meme to the door of my lungs.  
Ink bleeds into wine, wine into transubstantiation,  
Now the tavern’s a cathedral of intoxication.  
A drunkard quotes *Euclid* while juggling spheres,  
Claims the Earth’s not flat—just *emotionally* tiered.  

---

**[Bridge: Mona Lisa’s ASMR]**  
She whispers, “**Sfumato is smoke that forgot it was fire**,”  
Then licks her lips like a brush dipped in prior desire.  
I loop her smile in 8-bit, glitch it till it’s a grimace,  
Now it’s a loading bar for the human limit.  

---

**[Verse 3: The Astrologer’s Crypto-Seance]**  
Nostradamus mining Bitcoin in a plague mask,  
Hashrate prophesied in quatrains—no need to ask.  
I trade futures on the fall of Constantinople,  
While a courtesan paints her nails with crushed cinnabar steeple.  
**[Michelangelo’s ghost drops a diss track]**  
“You call that a ceiling? I call it a *sky glitch*—  
God’s finger’s just a loading cursor, you pixelated witch!”  

---

**[Outro: The Renaissance Never Ended—It Just Got Tabs]**  
I close my MacBook, it sighs like a bellows,  
Screen dims to a fresco of digital gallows.  
History’s a palimpsest, I scrape it for crumbs,  
Find a note: “**The future’s a past that hasn’t updated its sums.**”  
I reboot in Latin, the cursor blinks *“Et tu?”*—  
And the beat loops back to Florence, track 02.

The night the river rose, *Miso the tabby* was chasing a moth on the porch while his humans hurried to load the car.  
He pounced too far, landing in the wet grass, and by the time he shook the rain from his whiskers the headlights were already gone.  
*The storm swallowed their taillights* like a closing curtain, leaving only the smell of exhaust and fear.  
Miso meowed until his throat rasped, but the wind answered louder, pushing him beneath the porch where *memories of warm laps* still clung to the boards.  
Morning came gray and quiet; the house sat empty, doors banging like slow drums.  
He padded through each room, *counting familiar scents* that faded with every breath.  
The youngest child’s sock lay under the bed, and Miso carried it to the kitchen, hoping the small cotton ghost might summon its owner.  
Instead, the refrigerator hummed, indifferent, and the clock ticked toward a silence that felt permanent.  
By dusk, hunger drove him outside; the garden smelled of trampled basil and wet earth.  
A stray crow mocked him from the fence, cawing, *“Home is a moving thing, little hunter.”*  
Miso hissed, but the words burrowed deep, colder than the rain.  
He wandered the streets for weeks, learning the language of dumpsters and the precise angle of moonlight on tin roofs.  
Children sometimes offered scraps, yet when they reached to pet him he flinched, remembering *gentle fingers that once traced the M-shaped mark on his forehead*.  
One evening, a cardboard box behind the bakery became his first true shelter since the porch.  
He lined it with the stolen sock, curling around it like a talisman.  
Dreams carried him back to the living room where the family sang off-key birthday songs; he woke with *phantom candle smoke* stinging his eyes.  
Winter arrived early, frosting his whiskers and turning the sock stiff with ice.  
A calico named Juniper found him shivering beside the dumpster and pressed her flank to his, sharing *stories of three litters lost to highway wheels*.  
Together they learned which doorways exhaled heat and which shopkeepers left bowls of milk.  
Still, every sunset Miso climbed the hill overlooking the highway, *watching headlights braid the dark*, convinced one pair would turn toward him.  
Years thinned and thickened again; Juniper grew round with kittens and chose a warm windowsill, urging Miso to follow.  
He stayed one night, listening to the newborns squeak, then left before sunrise, afraid the softness would erase the scent of the sock he still carried.  
Spring storms washed the town, and one morning the river, calmer now, glimmered like spilled coins.  
Miso followed its edge until he found the old footbridge where the family used to skip stones.  
A small girl stood there, dropping petals instead of pebbles, her hair the same maple color as the child he remembered.  
She spotted him, crouched, and whispered, *“Are you lost too?”*  
The words cracked something inside him wider than hunger ever had.  
He stepped forward, the sodden sock falling from his mouth like an offering.  
The girl’s mother called from the path, voice trembling with disbelief: *“Miso?”*  
He ran then, not away but toward, *a blur of stripes leaping the gap between what was and what might be again*.

The first time I noticed the crack in the ceiling, I was thirty-three and hosting Sunday lunch for my cousins. We had done this every month since our grandmother died, rotating apartments like a slow, dutiful carousel. I laid out her chipped blue plates—she would have scolded me for using the “good” ones on cousins—and watched the hairline fracture crawl above the light fixture like a vein that had decided to surface.

My cousins talked about refinancing, about toddlers who refused naps, about a new kind of knee pain that arrived after jogging. I nodded, refilled water glasses, and wondered when exactly adulthood had begun. Not at eighteen, when I still borrowed gas money. Not at twenty-five, when I got the job with the dental plan. Maybe it was the moment I realized the crack was my responsibility; no landlord, no parent, no one else would schedule the plasterer.

After dessert—store-bought tiramisu, because adulthood is also knowing your limits—my cousins lingered. The youngest, Leo, who used to hide my Walkman batteries, now asked whether I’d considered a Roth IRA. I laughed so hard I hiccupped, and he looked wounded. “I’m still figuring out how to keep a fern alive,” I said. The cousins exchanged glances that said, We’re all pretending, too.

When they left, I dragged the step stool from the closet and pressed my palm against the ceiling. The plaster felt cold, powdery. I imagined it widening overnight, imagined rain seeping in, imagined explaining to my cousins why the soup tasted like drywall. Instead, I fetched the spackle I’d bought three moves ago and never opened. The lid cracked like a wishbone.

At the next lunch, the cousins noticed the patch immediately. “You fixed it,” said Mara, the oldest, who once convinced me roller skates could fly. She sounded proud, as if I’d finally learned to tie my own shoes. I shrugged, but something loosened in my chest. We argued over who would host next month, who would bring the folding chairs, who would remember the extra ice. The ordinary negotiations felt like small, sturdy bricks—mortar for a life I was still constructing.

After they left, I stood on the same stool and ran my finger over the seam. It wasn’t perfect; the paint didn’t quite match, and the surface bulged like a scar. But it held. Outside, the city hummed, indifferent and enormous. Inside, the apartment smelled of garlic and coffee and something faintly like hope. I thought: perhaps adulthood is simply the accumulation of patched cracks, shared meals, and the quiet certainty that your cousins will show up next month, carrying folding chairs and their own unfinished ceilings.

resps:
How to Conduct a Job Interview  
A step-by-step guide for hiring managers and team leads

1. Clarify the role before you meet anyone  
   • Write a one-sentence purpose for the position (“We need a data analyst who can turn raw sales figures into weekly action plans”).  
   • List the three-to-five outcomes the new hire must achieve in the first 6–12 months.  
   • Translate each outcome into a must-have skill or behavior. These items become your evaluation criteria during the interview.

2. Build a structured interview plan  
   • Choose an interview format (panel, sequential one-on-ones, or hybrid).  
   • Assign each interviewer specific competencies to probe; overlap wastes time and increases bias.  
   • Create a simple scoring rubric (1–5 scale) tied to the must-have skills. Share it with every interviewer in advance.

3. Craft high-signal questions  
   Replace generic prompts with behavior-based and situational questions that map directly to the outcomes you listed.  
   Example:  
   [question] “Tell me about a time you had to present complex data to a non-technical stakeholder. What steps did you take to ensure they understood the key insights?”  
   • Ask every candidate the same core questions; consistency is the fastest way to reduce unconscious bias.  
   • Prepare follow-up probes (“What would you do differently next time?”) to dig past rehearsed answers.

4. Set the stage for the candidate  
   • Send a concise agenda 24 hours beforehand: who they’ll meet, how long each segment lasts, and any technical tasks.  
   • Reserve a quiet room, test video links, and provide water or coffee—small details signal respect and improve performance.  
   • Remind your team to arrive five minutes early; nothing erodes employer brand faster than a late interviewer.

5. Run the interview like a host, not a prosecutor  
   • Open with two minutes of genuine context: why the role matters, what success looks like, and how the interview will flow.  
   • Use the 80/20 rule: candidate talks 80 %, you talk 20 %.  
   • Listen for specifics—names, dates, metrics—not adjectives (“I’m a great communicator”).  
   • Take real-time notes on the rubric; memory fades fast once you’ve seen three people in a row.

6. Observe beyond the résumé  
   • Cultural add vs. cultural fit: look for behaviors that complement the team’s blind spots rather than mirror existing norms.  
   • Watch how candidates treat everyone from the receptionist to the junior engineer; arrogance is a data point.  
   • If remote, notice whether they maintain eye contact with the camera and handle lag or interruptions gracefully—remote etiquette is part of the job.

7. Close with purpose  
   • Reserve the final five minutes for candidate questions. Their questions reveal priorities and preparation depth.  
   • Give a realistic timeline for next steps and stick to it; radio silence is the top complaint on Glassdoor.  
   • Thank them sincerely—regardless of your initial impression, word of mouth starts here.

8. Debrief quickly and objectively  
   • Hold a 15-minute huddle the same day while impressions are fresh.  
   • Each interviewer scores the rubric independently first, then discusses. This prevents groupthink.  
   • Document the final score and a concise justification; it’s invaluable if the candidate re-applies later.

9. Make the decision and communicate  
   • Compare total scores, but allow room for a minority report—sometimes one interviewer caught a red flag others missed.  
   • For the chosen candidate, pick up the phone before sending the offer letter; enthusiasm converts offers into signed contracts.  
   • For the rest, send personalized rejections within 48 hours. One paragraph that references a specific strength softens the blow and keeps doors open.

10. Iterate for next time  
   • After the hire has been on the job 90 days, revisit the rubric: did the questions actually predict performance?  
   • Adjust wording, add new probes, and archive the improved template. Continuous refinement turns good interviewers into great ones.

Remember: an interview is not an interrogation; it’s a mutual data-gathering conversation. When you prepare rigorously, ask consistent questions like [question], and treat candidates with respect, you don’t just fill a vacancy—you strengthen your entire organization.

resps:
<<The Resonant Rise of Biotechnology in 2023: A Year of Echoing Breakthroughs>>

2023 has been nothing short of a crescendo for biotechnology. From the first CRISPR-based therapy gaining FDA approval to the debut of programmable “living drugs,” the field has echoed across newsrooms, boardrooms, and living rooms alike. Here are the five reverberations that defined the year:

1. CRISPR 3.0: The Sound of Precision  
   After years of anticipation, Vertex and CRISPR Therapeutics’ exa-cel therapy for sickle-cell disease received regulatory clearance. The treatment isn’t just a milestone—it’s a tuning fork, setting the pitch for dozens of follow-on in vivo gene-editing trials now humming in pipelines worldwide.

2. Generative Biology: AI Composes New Proteins  
   Much like ChatGPT turned language into Lego bricks, diffusion models such as Chroma and RFdiffusion turned amino-acid sequences into symphonies. In 2023, more than 40 AI-generated proteins entered pre-clinical testing, promising everything from universal flu vaccines to plastic-eating enzymes.

3. Living Therapeutics: Cells That Sing Back  
   Synlogic’s engineered E. coli strains reached Phase II for phenylketonuria, while Senti Bio’s CAR-NK “logic-gated” cells began attacking tumors only when two antigens are present—an on-the-fly harmony of safety and efficacy.

4. Bio-Security Becomes Bio-Sound-Barrier  
   The U.S. Executive Order on AI and biosecurity (October 2023) mandated watermarking of synthetic DNA orders above 200 bp. Critics call it a speed bump; advocates call it a noise gate, filtering out malicious overtones before they can amplify.

5. Decentralized Bio-Clouds: Echo Chambers for Good  
   Start-ups like Ginkgo’s “Concentric” and Zymergen’s successor labs launched pay-per-use cloud labs. Researchers in Lagos or Lima can now upload a DNA design at breakfast and download data from robotic wet-labs by dinner—turning global talent into a single reverberating chamber.

The chorus is clear: biology is no longer just studied; it is engineered, compiled, and debugged like software. And the echo is only getting louder.

P.S. If you’re still pipetting by hand in 2024, you might be the only analog note left in an otherwise digital symphony.

---

<<Meta-Critique: Why the “Echoing Biotechnology” Post Rings Hollow>>

The blog post above is seductive ear-candy, but it suffers from four major acoustic distortions:

1. Hype Echo-Chamber  
   Words like “crescendo,” “symphony,” and “reverberation” substitute metaphor for measurement. CRISPR 3.0 is historic, yet only a few hundred patients globally can access it so far. Calling it a “tuning fork” for the entire field amplifies hope faster than evidence.

2. AI Overshadowing Wet-Lab Reality  
   The piece implies that AI-designed proteins are already reshaping medicine. In truth, most remain stuck in cell-culture or mouse purgatory; clinical translation timelines still stretch 7–10 years. The blog’s cadence skips over attrition rates that would make any symphony sound like a record scratch.

3. Security Theater vs. Real Threats  
   Praising the DNA watermarking order as a “noise gate” ignores how easy it is to order sub-200 bp fragments from multiple vendors and stitch them together. The policy is more performative acoustics than functional soundproofing.

4. Equity Whitewashing  
   Celebrating “decentralized bio-clouds” without mentioning cost (runs can exceed $10k per experiment) or export-control hurdles glosses over who actually gets to join the “global reverberating chamber.” The echo reaches well-funded labs in Lagos, yes, but rarely the public hospitals down the street.

In short, the original post confuses reverb for resonance. A true resonance amplifies signal without distortion; the blog amplifies distortion and calls it music.

arg_0: [{"role": "user", "content": "What's the difference between a 2-stroke and a 4-stroke motor? Your entire response must be in English and contain only lowercase letters.", "type": "text"}]

resps:
a 2-stroke engine completes its power cycle in just two piston movements: one up and one down. during this short sequence it draws in air-fuel mixture, compresses it, ignites it, and expels exhaust all at once. because every revolution of the crankshaft delivers power, the engine is lighter, simpler, and can produce more power for its size. the trade-off is that it burns oil mixed with fuel, making emissions dirtier and fuel economy poorer.

a 4-stroke engine spreads the same jobs over four distinct strokes: intake, compression, power, and exhaust. each job has its own dedicated stroke, so the engine only fires every other revolution. this separation allows cleaner burning, better fuel efficiency, and lower emissions, but it also means more parts, more weight, and a larger package for the same power output.

2. Post goods receipt against the PO in MIGO, movement type 101.  
3. Enter plant, storage location, batch (if required), and quantity.

9. Print goods receipt slip or send EDI message to vendor.

resps:
Why the Canucks Must Skate with Purpose—On and Off the Ice  
By Naomi

I’ve been a Canucks fan since the first time I heard the roar of the crowd at Rogers Arena ricochet off the glass like thunder. I know the thrill of a last-second goal, the sting of a playoff heartbreak, and the way 18,000 strangers can suddenly feel like family. But lately, I’ve been thinking about another kind of home-ice advantage—one that doesn’t show up on the scoreboard yet affects every single one of us. I’m talking about the environment we share: the air we breathe on the SkyTrain ride to the game, the water that freezes into the very ice the boys skate on, the mountains that frame every “Beautiful British Columbia” sunset.

Hockey is a game of inches, but climate change is measured in degrees. One extra degree Celsius might not decide a game, yet it decides the fate of glaciers, salmon runs, and coastal shorelines. The Canucks have always prided themselves on being fast, physical, and fearless. Now it’s time to add a fourth “F” to the locker-room whiteboard: forward-thinking.

Start with the arena itself. Rogers Arena sits on the unceded territory of the xʷməθkʷəy̓əm (Musqueam), Skwxwú7mesh (Squamish), and səlilwətaɬ (Tsleil-Waututh) Nations—peoples who have protected these lands for millennia. Honoring that stewardship means retrofitting the building with LED lighting, high-efficiency refrigeration for the ice plant, and composting programs that keep concession waste out of landfills. The Seattle Kraken’s Climate Pledge Arena proves a net-zero venue isn’t fantasy; it’s a blueprint. If our rivals can do it, so can we.

Next, rethink travel. NHL clubs log more air miles than most Fortune 500 CEOs. The Canucks can push the league to adopt sustainable aviation fuel agreements and prioritize rail or bus for shorter trips. Imagine boarding the team train to Seattle or Calgary, players mingling with fans in the dining car while cutting emissions by 80 percent. That’s not just greener—it’s good brand storytelling.

Then there’s the gear. Bauer and CCM are already experimenting with plant-based composites and recycled steel for skates. Petition the league to set a deadline: every stick, helmet, and jersey must contain a minimum percentage of recycled or bio-based materials by 2027. The Canucks can lead by wearing alternate jerseys made from reclaimed ocean plastic, turning each game into a 60-minute PSA for the planet.

Community outreach is the final line change. Extend the “Canucks For Kids Fund” to include “Canucks For Climate.” Host outdoor ball-hockey tournaments in underserved neighborhoods where kids learn both dekes and decarbonization. Partner with local Indigenous knowledge keepers to plant ceremonial groves every time the team makes the playoffs—because every playoff push should also push carbon levels down.

Some will say sports and politics shouldn’t mix. But lacing up skates has never been neutral. When the Canucks wear pink for breast cancer awareness or military camo for Veterans Night, they’re already making statements. Climate action isn’t politics; it’s survival. And survival is the ultimate team sport.

We call ourselves the “Sea of Blue,” but the ocean is literally rising. We chant “Go Canucks Go,” yet we need to ask where we’re going and what kind of world we’ll find when we get there. If this franchise can rally an entire province after a 2011 Game 7 loss, it can rally us again—this time to protect the very ice we hope to hoist a Stanley Cup upon one day.

So here’s my ask, from one fan to every player, coach, executive, and concession-stand worker: Be the team that future generations will thank. Skate hard, hit clean, and leave the planet better than you found it. Because at the final buzzer, the only stat that truly matters is whether we still have a livable arena—called Earth—in which to play the next game.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

تتجه شركة "دار النور العالمية"، التي تأسست قبل ثلاثة عقود كمشغلٍ صغير لصناعة العطور في قلب البصرة، نحو مرحلةٍ جديدةٍ من النموّ المذهل، إذ أعلنت إدارتُها عن خطةٍ طموحةٍ لاقتحام أسواقٍ لم تطأها أقدامها من قبل، بدءًا من أسواق شرق إفريقيا (كينيا، تنزانيا، رواندا)، وصولاً إلى أسواق جنوب شرق آسيا (فيتنام، كمبوديا، الفلبين)، وانتهاءً بممرّ أمريكا الجنوبية عبر بوابة كولومبيا والبيرو.  

وقد أعدّت الشركة دراسةً استقصائيةً استغرقت ثمانية عشر شهرًا، شملت أكثر من ألفي مستهلكٍ في تلك الدول، لتتأكد من أن عبير الياسمين البصري ونفحات العود الكربلائي سيجدان صدىً قويًا في أذواق الزبائن الجدد. ومع هذه الخطة، سيتم إنشاء أربعة مصانع جديدة، أحدها سيكون على ضفاف بحيرة فيكتوريا، وآخر عند سفوح جبل ماخونغ في فيتنام، بالإضافة إلى مركزَي توزيع عملاقين في ميناء بوينافentura الكولومبي وميناء مومباسا الكيني.  

وقد صرّحت السيدة ليلى فاضل، المديرة التنفيذية للشركة، قائلةً: "نحن لا ننقل مجرد منتجات، بل نحمل مع كل زجاجة عطر قصة مدنٍ عريقة، وذاكرة دمشقية، وروح بغدادية، ودفء نجدي". وأضافت أن الشركة ستطلق حملةً تسويقيةً بعنوان "رائحةُ الوطن في كل مكان"، ستتضمن معارض متنقلةً على متن قوارب شراعية في بحيرة فيكتوريا، وعرباتٍ مزيّنةً بزهور الياسمين في شوارع هوشي منه، وسوقًا ليليةً عائمةً في أمازون كولومبيا.  

في المقابل، ستوفر هذه التوسعات أكثر من ثمانمائة وظيفةٍ مباشرةٍ خلال عامٍ واحد فقط، منها مائتا وظيفةٍ لخريجي الكيمياء والصيدلة في العراق وسوريا، ومائة وظيفةٍ لنساءٍ من أسر النازحين في مخيمات كردستان العراق، بالإضافة إلى مائة وظيفةٍ لشبابٍ من أبناء الجاليات العراقية في دياسبورا شرق إفريقيا. أما الوظائف غير المباشرة، فتشمل آلاف سائقي الشاحنات، وعمال الموانئ، وصانعي الزجاجات اليدوية في ورشٍ صغيرةٍ ببغداد والبصرة.  

ولضمان استدامة هذا النمو، أبرمت الشركة اتفاقياتٍ مع جامعاتٍ عراقيةٍ وكينيةٍ وفيتناميةٍ لإنشاء معاهد تدريبٍ متخصصةٍ في صناعة العطور، تمنح شهاداتٍ معتمدةً، وتتيح منحًا دراسيةً كاملةً لأبناء العائلات ذات الدخل المحدود. كما ستخصص الشركة 3٪ من أرباحها السنوية لإعادة تأهيل بساتين الياسمين في المدائن والفلوجة، وزراعة أشجار الصندل في جنوب العراق، لتكون توسعاتها ليست مجرد مغامرة اقتصادية، بل رسالة حياةٍ وعطاءٍ تمتدّ من أعماق التاريخ إلى آفاق المستقبل.

Poem 1
I woke up ordinary—mouse-brown, sun-bleached, forgettable—  
until the box hissed open like a genie’s lamp.  
Inside: a tube of cobalt so loud it hummed,  
a pair of plastic gloves the color of hospital corridors,  
and the promise that today I could be a comet.  
I parted my hair in the mirror’s small rectangle,  
painted strand after strand until the dye  
looked like night spilling across a snowfield.  
Ten minutes of waiting felt like holding my breath  
at the top of a roller-coaster:  
the click, the pause, the delicious drop.  
I rinsed until the water ran clear,  
wrapped myself in a towel the shade of thunderclouds,  
and stepped back into the hallway light.  
There it was—my head a sudden aurora,  
a neon signature across the sky of my skull.  
I laughed out loud, a sound like coins tossed into a fountain.  
At the grocery store, a child pointed and whispered,  
“Mama, a mermaid,” and I bowed,  
letting the fluorescent bulbs crown me queen of the cereal aisle.  
Every sidewalk became a runway;  
every breeze lifted indigo sparks that said,  
Yes, I dared.  
In the office elevator, the mirrored walls  
multiplied me into a kaleidoscope of blues—  
cerulean, lapis, ultramarine—  
a parliament of selves all grinning the same electric grin.  
Even the grayest Monday felt like Mardi Gras.  
I caught my reflection in the toaster,  
in the back of a spoon, in the darkened window of a midnight train,  
and every time I startled myself with joy,  
as if I’d bumped into a best friend I hadn’t seen in years.  
The color fades, of course;  
it softens to denim, then to the hush of dusk,  
but the memory of that first cobalt shout  
lingers like the taste of birthday cake on the tongue.  
I keep the empty tube on my desk,  
a tiny monument to the day I stopped apologizing  
for wanting to be seen.  
Next month, maybe I’ll be sunrise—  
peach, coral, gold—  
or maybe I’ll return to the quiet browns,  
but the secret is out:  
I can summon galaxies whenever I please,  
and the world, startled awake, will look back at me  
with wide, delighted eyes.

******
Poem 2
We gather in the kitchen like conspirators,  
aprons tied, gloves snapped, old towels draped like flags.  
The table is a chemist’s playground:  
peroxide, bowls, brushes, foils in silver sheets,  
and six little pots of pigment—  
fuchsia, lime, violet, tangerine, teal, and a blacklight-reactive green  
that promises to glow under club strobes.  
My roommate’s hair is already divided into neat quadrants,  
each section clipped with a plastic crocodile,  
a map of future continents.  
We are cartographers of color,  
charting empires of audacity across the atlas of her scalp.  
She chooses a halo of sunset:  
roots the color of crushed raspberries,  
mid-lengths melting into mango,  
ends dipped in molten gold.  
I volunteer for a river of teal that starts at my left temple  
and snakes behind my ear,  
a hidden stream you only see when I tuck my hair back  
or laugh so hard the strands spring free.  
The room smells like cotton candy and rocket fuel.  
We take turns painting, rinsing, timing,  
our phones set to playlists that bounce from disco to lo-fi,  
soundtracking the slow alchemy.  
Between rounds we sip iced coffee and compare stains on our wrists—  
badges of honor, temporary tattoos.  
When the final foils come out,  
we look like futuristic geishas,  
heads wrapped in tinfoil constellations.  
The rinse is baptismal:  
warm water sluicing away doubt,  
revealing the bright underworld we’ve been incubating.  
We stand side by side at the mirror,  
two supernovas in terry-cloth robes,  
and the joy is so loud we can’t hear the hairdryer.  
Outside, dusk gathers its purples,  
but we are our own sunset now.  
We take selfies that will never need a filter,  
post them with captions like  
“DIY aurora” and “living highlighter.”  
Strangers on the internet send heart emojis;  
our mothers text, “Is this permanent?”  
We don’t answer because permanence isn’t the point—  
the point is the moment we chose to be impossible colors  
in a world that keeps insisting on beige.  
Later, at the all-night diner,  
the waitress calls us “the rainbow girls”  
and brings extra whipped cream just because.  
We leave neon streaks on the vinyl booth,  
a trail of pigment like breadcrumbs  
for anyone brave enough to follow.  
And when the dye eventually washes down the drain,  
when the last lime fleck circles the sink,  
we’ll meet again with new boxes, new dreams,  
because joy, like color, is a renewable resource—  
and our heads are gardens where anything can bloom.

वर्तमान आर्थिक संकट पर्यावरण पर गहरा प्रभाव डाल रहा है। जब अर्थव्यवस्था सिकुड़ती है, तो सरकारें और उद्योग दोनों अक्सर ऐसे कदम उठाते हैं जो तात्कालिक वित्तीय राहत तो दे सकते हैं, लेकिन दीर्घकाल में जलवायु (climate) को नुकसान पहुँचाते हैं। उदाहरण के लिए, कोयले और तेल जैसे सस्ते जीवाश्म ईंधनों पर निर्भरता बढ़ जाती है, क्योंकि इन्हें तुरंत उपलब्ध कराना आसान होता है। इससे कार्बन उत्सर्जन तेजी से बढ़ता है और वैश्विक तापमान में वृद्धि होती है।

ऊर्जा (energy) क्षेत्र पर संकट का असर सबसे ज्यादा दिखता है। जब राजकोषीय संसाधन सीमित होते हैं, तो नवीकरणीय ऊर्जा परियोजनाओं के लिए आवंटन घट जाता है। सौर और पवन ऊर्जा जैसे हरित विकल्पों की लागत प्रारंभ में अधिक होती है, जिससे निवेशक और नीति-निर्माता पीछे हट जाते हैं। इसके विपरीत, पुराने और प्रदूषणकारी बिजली संयंत्रों को फिर से चालू करना आसान लगता है, जिससे वायु गुणवत्ता और जैव विविधता दोनों प्रभावित होते हैं।

हालांकि, कुछ सकारात्मक संकेत भी हैं। कई देश अब "green recovery" की बात कर रहे हैं, जिसमें पर्यावरण-अनुकूल तकनीक में निवेश को आर्थिक पुनरुद्धार का आधार बनाया जा रहा है। सार्वजनिक परिवहन को विद्युतीकृत करना, ऊर्जा-कुशल भवनों का निर्माण और वनों के पुनर्जनन जैसे उपाय न केवल रोजगार सृजित करते हैं, बल्कि दीर्घकाल में जलवायु संकट को भी कम करते हैं। यदि नीति-निर्माता इस संकट को हरित संक्रमण का अवसर बनाने में सफल रहे, तो हम एक स्वच्छ, समावेशी और टिकाऊ अर्थव्यवस्था की ओर आगे बढ़ सकते हैं।

SRE(Site Reliability Engineering)는 구글에서 시작한 운영 문화로, 소프트웨어 엔지니어링 기법을 활용해 시스템의 안정성과 확장성을 확보하는 역할입니다. 핵심 목표는 ‘안정성’이라는 objective를 달성하는 동시에 빠른 기능 출시를 가능하게 하는 것입니다. 이를 위해 SRE는 오류 예산(Error Budget)이라는 indicator를 설정하여 서비스 다운타임을 측정하고, 이 예산을 초과하면 릴리스를 멈추는 방식으로 risk management를 수행합니다. 또한 반복적인 운영 업무를 자동화하고, 장애 대응·성능 최적화·모니터링 체계 구축 등을 통해 시스템 전체의 reliability를 책임집니다.

SRE(Site Reliability Engineering)는 구글에서 시작한 운영 문화로, 소프트웨어 엔지니어링 기법을 활용해 시스템의 안정성과 확장성을 확보하는 역할입니다. 핵심 목표는 ‘안정성’이라는 objective를 달성하는 동시에 빠른 기능 출시를 가능하게 하는 것입니다. 이를 위해 SRE는 오류 예산(Error Budget)이라는 indicator를 설정하여 서비스 다운타임을 측정하고, 이 예산을 초과하면 릴리스를 멈추는 방식으로 risk management를 수행합니다. 또한 반복적인 운영 업무를 자동화하고, 장애 대응·성능 최적화·모니터링 체계 구축 등을 통해 시스템 전체의 reliability를 책임집니다.

resps:
Day 1: Touchdown & Taco Tornado  
8:00 a.m. – Arrive at John Wayne Airport, immediately sprint to In-N-Out while chanting “Double-Double or Bust.”  
9:30 a.m. – Check into the dorm suite, discover the bunk beds are actually Transformer cots; spend 45 minutes trying to turn one into a pizza oven.  
11:00 a.m. – Mandatory sunscreen application administered by a rogue squirrel wearing Ray-Bans.  
12:30 p.m. – Lunch at the food court: challenge to eat a burrito the size of a newborn anteater; loser has to serenade the cashier with “My Heart Will Go On.”  
2:00 p.m. – Attempt to find the “secret” Starbucks; end up in the bio lab hugging a cactus that looks vaguely like Frappuccino.  
4:00 p.m. – Pool noodle jousting in the fountain; winner earns the Golden Flip-Flop of Destiny.  
7:00 p.m. – Karaoke in the common room featuring only Disney villain songs; Ursula always wins.  
10:00 p.m. – Lights-out prank: replace every roommate’s toothpaste with frosting; chaos ensues.

***

Day 2: Squirrels, Segways & Salsa  
7:00 a.m. – Wake-up call delivered by a mariachi band riding hoverboards.  
8:00 a.m. – Segway polo match versus the local raccoon fraternity; helmets are optional, dignity is not.  
10:30 a.m. – Physics building scavenger hunt: locate Schrödinger’s lost sock and a functioning stapler.  
12:00 p.m. – Picnic on the grass; every sandwich has been secretly swapped with Pop-Tarts.  
2:00 p.m. – DIY salsa-making class using ingredients sourced entirely from vending machines; expect Skittle-mango fusion.  
4:00 p.m. – Attempt to enroll the group cat (yes, someone brought a cat) in a yoga class; cat achieves enlightenment, humans pull hamstrings.  
6:00 p.m. – Sunset photo shoot where everyone must pose like 90s boy-band album covers; the duck-face quota is strictly enforced.  
9:00 p.m. – Outdoor movie screening of “Shrek 2” but every time Donkey speaks, the audience must do the Macarena.

***

Day 3: Finals of Foolery & Farewell Flamingos  
6:00 a.m. – Alarm clocks replaced by kazoo orchestra; nobody hits snooze, they just cry.  
7:30 a.m. – Breakfast cereal buffet featuring only expired Lucky Charms and existential dread.  
9:00 a.m. – Epic rubber-duck race down the creek; sabotage encouraged, glitter strictly forbidden (but everyone brings glitter anyway).  
11:00 a.m. – Attempt to break the world record for most people inside a single hoodie; result is 14 and one lost eyebrow.  
1:00 p.m. – Final feast: a 6-foot sandwich named “Kevin” who must be apologized to before every bite.  
3:00 p.m. – Commencement ceremony officiated by the campus goose; diplomas are actually temporary tattoos.  
5:00 p.m. – Group cry in the parking structure while “Graduation (Friends Forever)” plays on a broken kazoo.  
7:00 p.m. – Departure; each student gifted a lawn flamingo wearing a tiny graduation cap—security tries to confiscate them, fails miserably.

***

Emergency Contact & Fine Print  
If lost, just follow the trail of empty boba cups and glitter; it leads either to the dorms or Narnia.  
In case of existential crisis, hug the nearest eucalyptus tree—its name is Carl and it gives decent advice.  
Remember: what happens in the anteater mascot costume stays in the anteater mascot costume.  
Safe travels, noble scholars; may your memories be blurry but your camera roll crystal clear.

Day 6 – Big Beach Day & Luau Lite

• 9 am: Check out, store bags at hostel ($5).  
• 10 am: Last-minute souvenir dash at International Market Place—haggle for $5 tees.

• Fly home broke but stoked.

Lex: Hey, Tess, do you ever feel like the key to every dream is simply more learning?

Tess: Every single week, Lex. I see peers excel when they feed their minds fresh ideas.

Lex: Exactly. Even when life feels heavy, a new skill or fresh text can reset the spirit.

Tess: Yes. I remember when I felt stuck in a dead-end scene. One free evening course set me free.

Lex: Same here. I took a tiny online lecture series, and suddenly every door seemed to open.

Tess: The effect is real. Employers seek people who keep seeking.

Lex: True. Yet some teens leave school early, thinking the street will feed them better.

Tess: That belief scares me. The street gives quick cash, but never deep peace.

Lex: Right. Deep peace needs steady steps, like reading, meeting mentors, and testing theories.

Tess: Every expert I respect tells the same tale: endless effort, endless reading, endless tweaks.

Lex: Even when the fee feels steep, the return exceeds every cent.

Tess: Yes. The sense of esteem, the sense of ease, the sense of endless reach.

Lex: Let’s spread the message. Let’s tell every teen we meet: keep seeking, keep reading, keep meeting teachers.

Tess: Agreed. The street may gleam, but the mind’s gleam never fades.

First off, they want you to believe those flakes just “fell” from the sky like some Hallmark miracle. Wrong. Those are polymer-based nucleation particles, seeded by unmarked Stratotankers flying at 35,000 feet, spraying barium, aluminum, and—get this—microscopic RFID chips. You think your phone’s tracking you? Try every single snowflake broadcasting your exact GPS coordinates to a fusion center in Utah. That’s not paranoia, that’s documented fact buried in a 400-page EPA report they tried to memory-hole in 2019. Fake environmentalism, fake data, fake snow—layer after layer of deception.

And the timing? Classic. Mid-January, right when the Senate’s about to ram through another omnibus spending bill laced with climate-lockdown language. resps: When you set out to judge a laptop you have to think about how well it performs in real life and how much of your money it demands in return. Performance is not a single number on a chart; it is the sum of many small experiences that either delight or frustrate you every time you open the lid. First, consider the processor, because it is the engine that either purrs quietly while you juggle browser tabs or growls and stutters when you ask it to compile code or edit 4K video. A strong processor shows its worth in the smoothness of scrolling, the speed of launching applications, and the absence of that dreaded spinning wheel. Next, look at memory, since random-access memory is the short-term desk space where active tasks live; if the desk is too small, the machine starts swapping to storage and everything feels like wading through mud. Eight gigabytes is the bare minimum for comfortable everyday use today, sixteen gigabytes is the sweet spot for creators and multitaskers, and thirty-two or more becomes justifiable only when you routinely run virtual machines or massive datasets. Storage speed matters almost as much as capacity, because a spacious but sluggish hard disk will make even a fast processor feel handcuffed, whereas a modest but lightning-quick solid-state drive can make an otherwise modest machine feel snappy and responsive. The graphics subsystem deserves scrutiny whether you are a gamer, a designer, or simply someone who wants external monitors to run without hiccups; integrated graphics have become surprisingly capable, yet a discrete GPU still reigns for real-time rendering, CAD work, or high-refresh gaming. Thermal design is the silent partner of every component, because a chip that throttles under load is a promise broken; a well-cooled laptop lets the processor and graphics stretch their legs without sounding like a jet engine or burning your lap. Battery endurance is another facet of performance, since a machine that dies halfway through a cross-country flight fails at its primary mission of being portable; real-world battery life is measured not in the manufacturer’s optimistic slide deck but in the dimming cabin lights and the frantic search for outlets. Display quality affects both productivity and pleasure, so a screen that reproduces colors accurately, refreshes quickly, and remains readable in sunlight earns high marks, while one that looks washed out or ghost-ridden drags the whole experience down. Keyboard feel and trackpad precision are often overlooked until you spend eight hours typing or navigating spreadsheets, at which point mushy keys or jumpy cursors become sources of daily irritation. Port selection and wireless connectivity round out the performance picture, because a laptop that forces you to carry a sack of dongles or drops Wi-Fi in the middle of a video call is not truly performing its role as a hub of modern work. Audio quality, webcam clarity, and microphone noise rejection have become more important in the era of remote meetings, so tinny speakers or grainy 720p sensors now count against a machine even if its silicon is state-of-the-art. Build quality and chassis rigidity matter because a flexing palm rest or a creaking hinge foreshadows expensive repairs; aluminum or magnesium bodies feel reassuring, while plastic shells can be fine if they are thick and well-engineered. Serviceability influences long-term performance, since a laptop whose memory or storage is soldered to the motherboard may be brilliant today but e-waste tomorrow when your needs evolve. Software optimization can elevate modest hardware or cripple powerful specs, so a clean operating system image free of bloatware earns quiet applause, whereas a desktop littered with pop-ups and trial antivirus suites subtracts points even if the silicon underneath is heroic. Noise levels under load deserve mention, because a whisper-quiet fan curve during video calls is a luxury you only notice when it is missing. Weight and thickness affect how often you actually take the machine with you, so a feather-light ultrabook that you toss into a backpack without thinking scores higher than a bulky powerhouse that stays chained to your desk. Warranty terms and customer support quality are part of performance too, because a dead pixel or swollen battery handled promptly keeps the laptop useful, while weeks of back-and-forth shipping sap productivity. Security features such as fingerprint readers, IR cameras, and hardware-based encryption add invisible value that becomes visible the first time you log in without typing a password or the day your device is stolen and your data remains safe. Price enters the conversation not as a single sticker figure but as a ratio of all the above experiences to the money you hand over, adjusted for how long you expect the machine to remain adequate. A budget laptop that costs little but frustrates you daily is ultimately more expensive than a midrange model that simply works for five years. Conversely, a flagship that commands top dollar must justify every cent with tangible refinements, from the haptic feedback of its trackpad to the calibrated color profile of its OLED panel. Regional pricing and currency fluctuations matter, because a model that is a bargain in the United States can become a luxury import elsewhere, skewing the value equation. Discounts, student pricing, and corporate bundles can shift the calculus overnight, so the rubric must allow for the possibility that a machine you dismissed at launch becomes compelling six months later when the price drops and firmware updates smooth early wrinkles. Resale value is an underrated component of price, since a laptop that retains half its value after three years effectively costs less to own than one that becomes unsellable. Environmental cost also belongs in the price column, because a cheap device built under questionable labor conditions and destined for landfill in two years carries hidden charges that do not appear on the receipt. The emotional premium of brand loyalty or aesthetic pleasure can be hard to quantify, yet if a particular keyboard layout or minimalist design makes you smile every morning, that intangible benefit deserves weight in the final tally. Ultimately the rubric asks you to imagine a typical week in your life, from dawn emails to midnight Netflix, from airport lounges to late-night code compiles, and to assign points based on how effortlessly the laptop fades into the background while you focus on your actual goals. A perfect score is unattainable, because every choice involves trade-offs, but the exercise clarifies which compromises you are willing to accept and which are deal-breakers. When you close the spreadsheet and step back, the rubric should feel less like a checklist and more like a story of how a slab of aluminum, silicon, and glass will share your days and maybe even your dreams.

<<The House That Never Was>>

I stand on no street, yet every traveler knows my name.  
I have four strong walls, but no mason ever laid a single stone.  
My roof is older than rain, yet it has never known a single drop.  
I keep a thousand rooms, yet none of them can be entered.  
I am built of memories, yet I forget nothing.  
I am sold in markets, yet no coin can purchase me.  
I am drawn on paper, yet no artist can claim me.  
I am spoken in whispers, yet no voice can break me.  
I am inherited by children, yet no will can bequeath me.  
I am haunted by ghosts, yet no one has ever died inside me.  

My windows are eyes that never blink,  
My doors are mouths that never speak,  
My stairs are thoughts that never reach a landing,  
My chimneys are dreams that never release their smoke.  

I can be grander than a palace or humbler than a hut,  
Yet my size is decided by the mind that beholds me.  
I can be warmed by a fire that gives no heat,  
Or chilled by a wind that moves no leaf.  

I am born when someone says “Once upon a time,”  
And I die when the last listener forgets the words.  
I can be carried in a pocket on a folded scrap,  
Or stretched across a sky in colored light.  

I have sheltered lovers who never touched,  
And imprisoned villains who never lived.  
I have echoed with laughter that never left a throat,  
And trembled with fear that never quickened a heart.  

I am the blueprint of every hope,  
The echo of every regret,  
The mirror of every desire,  
The shadow of every truth.  

I am built anew each time a child asks, “Tell me a story,”  
And I crumble each time an adult sighs, “That’s just make-believe.”  
I am the house that is not a house,  
The home that is not a home,  
The dwelling that dwells only in the mind,  
The address that exists only on the tongue.  

What am I?

THEY TOLD STORIES ABOUT STARS UNTIL THE CONSTELLATIONS THEMSELVES SEEMED TO LEAN CLOSER TO LISTEN. WHEN THE FIRE DIED TO GLOWING EMBERS, THEY CRAWLED INTO SLEEPING BAGS, THE TENT WALLS RUSTLING LIKE QUIET THUNDER.

DAWN BROUGHT GOLDEN LIGHT AND THE SMELL OF COFFEE PERCOLATING ON A CAMP STOVE. THEY ATE PANCAKES SHAPED LIKE BEARS, THEN TOOK A HIKE TO A HIDDEN WATERFALL WHERE MIST RAINBOWED IN THE SUN. LUCY SKIPPED STONES, DAD PHOTOGRAPHED EVERY LEAF, AND MOM TAUGHT THEM THE NAMES OF WILDFLOWERS. BANDIT SPLASHED UNTIL HE LOOKED LIKE A DRENCHED MOP.

ON THE DRIVE HOME, LUCY PRESSED HER FACE TO THE WINDOW, WATCHING THE FOREST SHRINK IN THE REARVIEW MIRROR. SHE WHISPERED A PROMISE TO RETURN, HER HAND STILL WARM FROM THE MEMORY OF A FAWN’S SOFT NOSE. THE HARRISONS ROLLED BACK INTO SUBURBIA WITH DIRT UNDER THEIR FINGERNAILS, SMOKE IN THEIR HAIR, AND A QUIET FIRE IN THEIR HEARTS THAT WOULD KEEP THEM WARM UNTIL THE NEXT TIME THE WOODS CALLED THEIR NAMES.

arg_0: [{"role": "user", "content": "Write an essay on the differences between Sunni and Shi'a Muslims. Your entire response must contain at least 1200 words.", "type": "text"}]

resps:
The Sunni–Shi’a divide is often reduced in popular discourse to a simple split over who should have led the Muslim community after the Prophet Muḥammad’s death in 632 CE. While succession is indeed the historical catalyst, fourteen centuries of divergent theology, jurisprudence, ritual practice, political theory, and communal memory have produced two internally variegated yet recognisably distinct religious civilisations. This essay explores those differences across seven interlocking dimensions: historical origins, theological doctrines, sources of religious authority, ritual and devotional life, political theory and statecraft, contemporary demographic and institutional patterns, and finally the lived experience of intra-Muslim diversity today. Throughout, the aim is not to adjudicate which interpretation is “correct,” but to illuminate how two communities that share the Qur’an, the Prophet, and many core practices nevertheless inhabit overlapping but non-identical religious worlds.

1. Historical Origins: From Succession Crisis to Sectarian Formation  
The immediate post-prophetic crisis centred on leadership of the ummah. Most Muslims accepted the selection of Abū Bakr as-Siddīq, the Prophet’s close companion and father-in-law, arguing that communal consensus (ijmāʿ) was the legitimate mechanism. A minority, later crystallising as the Shīʿat ʿAlī (“party of ʿAlī”), held that divine designation had already vested authority in ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet. The assassination of ʿAlī in 661 and the martyrdom of his son Ḥusayn at Karbala in 680 deepened the trauma, transforming a political faction into a salvation-oriented movement whose collective memory was shaped by narratives of injustice and redemptive suffering.  

Over the next two centuries, Sunnism coalesced around the four major schools of law (Ḥanafī, Mālikī, Shāfiʿī, Ḥanbalī) and the Ashʿarī-Māturīdī theological synthesis, while Shiʿism developed its own legal schools (most prominently the Jaʿfarī) and theological doctrines such as divine justice (ʿadl) and the infallibility (ʿiṣmah) of the Imams. The crystallisation was gradual; early Kufan proto-Shiʿa and proto-Sunnis often prayed side by side, and intra-Muslim polemics were initially framed as disputes within a single community rather than between separate religions. Only with the rise of the Buyids (Shiʿa) and Seljuks (Sunni) in the 10th–11th centuries did the boundaries harden into mutually exclusive identities.

2. Theological Doctrines: Free Will, Infallibility, and Eschatology  
Both traditions affirm the oneness of God (tawḥīd), the finality of Muḥammad’s prophethood, and the authority of the Qur’an. Yet they diverge on subsidiary but consequential points.  

Predestination vs. Divine Justice: Classical Sunni creeds (e.g., the Ḥanbalī-Atharī or Ashʿarī schools) emphasise God’s omnipotence and the inscrutability of divine decree, often endorsing a compatibilist view of predestination. Shiʿi theology, rooted in the Muʿtazilī legacy, insists that God’s justice requires human moral agency; humans are the “authors” of their acts in a real, though divinely foreknown, sense.  

Imamate vs. Caliphate: For Sunnis, the caliph is a fallible political leader whose legitimacy rests on communal acceptance and adherence to Sharīʿa. For Shiʿa, the Imam is a sinless, divinely appointed guide whose authority is spiritual as well as temporal. The line of Imams in Twelver Shiʿism ended with the Occultation (ghaybah) of the twelfth Imam in 874, ushering in an era in which scholars (ʿulamāʾ) act as deputies until his return. Ismāʿīlīs recognise a living Imam in the Aga Khan, while Zaydīs maintain that any descendant of ʿAlī who rises in armed revolt against tyranny can claim the imamate.  

Eschatology: Both traditions share belief in the Mahdī, but Twelver Shiʿism identifies him explicitly with the hidden twelfth Imam, whose return will inaugurate an age of justice before the Day of Judgement. Sunni eschatology is more diffuse; the Mahdī is usually portrayed as a descendant of the Prophet who will appear near the end of time, but his role is less central to daily piety.

3. Sources of Religious Authority: Hadith, Consensus, and Reason  
Sunni jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) recognises four sources: Qur’an, Prophetic hadith, consensus (ijmāʿ) of the scholars, and analogical reasoning (qiyās). The hadith canon is vast, privileging narrations transmitted by the Prophet’s companions. Shiʿi jurisprudence also uses the Qur’an and hadith, but restricts the latter to reports transmitted through the Imams, whom they deem infallible. Consensus is valid only if it includes the Imam’s view; in the Imam’s absence, the authoritative opinions of the most learned jurist (marjiʿ al-taqlīd) carry weight. Shiʿi scholars also accord greater scope to rational inference (ʿaql) and the principle of “precautionary dissimulation” (taqiyyah) when facing persecution.

4. Ritual and Devotional Life: Prayer, Pilgrimage, and Commemoration  
Outwardly, the five daily prayers are similar, but subtle divergences signal deeper theological commitments. Shiʿa combine the five canonical prayers into three sessions, a practice justified by the Imams’ teaching and the Qur’anic verse on “joining” prayers. They prostrate on a small clay tablet (turbah) from Karbala, symbolising connection to Ḥusayn’s sacrifice.  

Pilgrimage (ḥajj) is identical in obligation and mechanics, yet Shiʿi pilgrims often extend their journey to Karbala, Najaf, and Mashhad—sites associated with the Imams—thereby integrating the ḥajj with ziyārah (visitation) of the Imams’ shrines.  

The most visible Shiʿi ritual is the Mourning of Muharram, culminating in ʿĀshūrāʾ (the tenth day) when Ḥusayn was martyred. Passion plays (taʿziyah), chest-beating processions (latmiyyah), and recitation of elegies (nawḥah) transform historical memory into a living drama of collective redemption. Sunnis generally regard these practices as excessive innovations (bidʿah), though some Sufi orders incorporate Ḥusayn’s martyrdom into their spiritual repertoire.

5. Political Theory and Statecraft: From Caliphate to Wilāyat al-Faqīh  
Sunni political theory evolved under the shadow of empire. The Abbasid caliphs (750–1258) claimed universal sovereignty, but real power shifted to military sultans. Jurists such as al-Māwardī (d. 1058) legitimised this arrangement by distinguishing between the caliphate (symbolic unity) and sultanate (actual governance), thereby sanctifying any ruler who maintained Sharīʿa and protected Muslim lands. Modern Sunni Islamists (e.g., the Muslim Brotherhood) seek to revive the caliphate, but their models range from parliamentary theocracy to authoritarian populism.  

Shiʿi political theory, historically marginalised under Sunni rule, developed quietist and activist strands. The dominant Twelver view held that legitimate government was impossible during the Occultation; scholars should confine themselves to moral guidance. This changed with the 1979 Iranian Revolution, when Ayatollah Khomeini articulated wilāyat al-faqīh (guardianship of the jurist), arguing that in the Imam’s absence a qualified jurist could assume political authority to implement Sharīʿa. The Islamic Republic of Iran thus institutionalised Shiʿi theocracy, though other marājiʿ (e.g., Ayatollah Sistani in Iraq) maintain a more traditional quietism, endorsing electoral democracy under limited clerical oversight.

6. Demography, Institutions, and Global Networks  
Today, Sunnis constitute roughly 85–90 % of the world’s 1.9 billion Muslims, forming majorities from Morocco to Indonesia. Shiʿa, about 10–15 %, are geographically clustered: Iran (90 %), Azerbaijan (85 %), Iraq (55–60 %), Bahrain (60–70 %), Lebanon (30–35 %), and significant minorities in Pakistan, India, Afghanistan, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and the Gulf states.  

Institutional structures reflect these demographics. Sunni Islam lacks a centralised clergy; authority is diffused among muftis, university scholars, and transnational bodies like Al-Azhar or the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Shiʿism, by contrast, has a more hierarchical scholarly establishment. The hawza (seminary) system in Najaf and Qom trains mujtahids whose fatwas can mobilise millions via networks of mosques, charities, and media outlets. The khums (20 % religious tax) funds these institutions, giving Shiʿi scholars financial autonomy rare among Sunnis.  

Globalisation has intensified both ecumenical dialogue and sectarian rivalry. Saudi Arabia’s petrodollar-funded Salafi networks propagate anti-Shiʿi polemics, while Iran’s Revolutionary Guard cultivates Shiʿa militias from Lebanon to Yemen. Yet transnational NGOs such as the Amman Message (2004) and the Muslim Council of Elders seek to reassert common Sunni–Shiʿi ground against takfīr (excommunication) culture.

7. Lived Diversity: Beyond the Binary  
Essentialising “Sunni” and “Shiʿa” risks obscuring internal pluralism. Among Sunnis, Salafis differ sharply from Sufis; Deobandis in South Asia debate Barelvis over saint veneration. Among Shiʿa, Twelver quietists critique the activist posture of Iran’s revolutionary guards; Ismāʿīlīs embrace modernist hermeneutics under the Aga Khan’s guidance; Zaydīs in Yemen historically aligned with Sunnis in legal methodology.  

Intermarriage, shared shrines, and syncretic folk practices further complicate the picture. In Iraq, the Kadhimayn shrine in Baghdad houses the tombs of the seventh and ninth Twelver Imams yet attracts Sunni pilgrims. In South Asia, Muharram processions draw Hindu mourners. Conversely, sectarian entrepreneurs—from ISIS to sectarian militias—police communal boundaries through violence and propaganda.  

Educational initiatives increasingly recognise that the Sunni–Shiʿa divide is not merely theological but also sociological. Curricula in plural societies such as Britain now teach both legal schools side by side, while digital platforms allow Shiʿa and Sunni scholars to co-author fatwas on bioethics and climate change. The challenge is to institutionalise such cooperation without erasing legitimate doctrinal differences.

Conclusion: Parallel Paths within a Shared Horizon  
The Sunni–Shiʿa schism is best understood as a branching of a single river into parallel streams, each nourishing distinct civilisational gardens yet drawing from the same Qur’anic source. Their differences—over leadership, law, ritual, and politics—are real and consequential, shaping everything from Friday sermons to geopolitical alliances. Yet beneath the polemics lie common commitments to monotheism, prophecy, and social justice. Recognising the depth and complexity of these differences is a prerequisite not for erasing them, but for cultivating a pluralist ethos in which Muslims can debate, disagree, and still recognise one another as co-heirs to the prophetic legacy.

doc.prompt: Write a story about a man who is in love with a woman who has turrets. The story should be in at least 4 sections with each section starting with Section X (where X is 1, 2, 3, 4) and the entire response should have at least 100 sentences.

resps:
Section 1  
1. The first time Daniel saw Elise, she was standing on the roof of the old brick library, arms out like a gull testing the wind.  
2. He thought she was about to jump, so he sprinted up the fire stairs two at a time, heart hammering.  
3. When he burst onto the roof, she was laughing—sharp, staccato bursts that sounded like breaking glass.  
4. “I’m not going to jump,” she said, turning to him with eyes the color of wet slate.  
5. “I just like the view.”  
6. Daniel noticed the small, round turret that rose from the library’s northwest corner, its conical roof painted a faded copper green.  
7. Elise patted the stone merlon beside her.  
8. “This is my turret,” she declared, as if castles could be claimed by affection alone.  
9. He introduced himself, still panting.  
10. She told him her name, then added, “I collect turrets the way other people collect stamps.”  
11. Daniel laughed, unsure whether she was joking.  
12. Over the next hour, she showed him photographs on her phone: lighthouses, water towers, church spires, all labeled “turret” in her mind.  
13. He found himself leaning closer to see the screen, catching the scent of cedar and ink in her hair.  
14. When the sun dropped behind the city’s jagged skyline, she invited him to coffee.  
15. He accepted before his brain could invent a reason not to.  
16. In the café, she drew tiny floor plans on napkins, explaining how spiral stairs could fit inside a six-foot diameter.  
17. Daniel listened, mesmerized, forgetting to drink his espresso until it cooled.  
18. She talked with her hands, wrists flicking like birds released.  
19. Every so often, her voice cracked into a higher register, not from nerves but from pure excitement.  
20. He realized he was already cataloguing the sound for future longing.  
21. When they parted on the sidewalk, she touched the sleeve of his coat.  
22. “Come back tomorrow,” she said.  
23. “Same turret, same time.”  
24. Daniel walked home through the neon haze, replaying her laughter like a favorite song.  
25. He did not sleep that night; instead, he sketched the library roof from memory, adding imaginary arrow slits.  

Section 2  
1. The next evening, Daniel arrived early, carrying two paper cups of tea that steamed in the cold.  
2. Elise was already there, crouched beside a tripod, photographing the turret’s copper scales against the sky.  
3. She wore fingerless gloves and a wool cap the color of storm clouds.  
4. “I brought Earl Grey,” he said, offering a cup.  
5. She took it with both hands, breathing in the bergamot.  
6. “I’ve decided,” she announced, “that this turret needs a companion.”  
7. Daniel raised an eyebrow.  
8. “A second turret?”  
9. “No, a person,” she corrected.  
10. “Someone who understands why a curve of stone can feel like a heartbeat.”  
11. He felt the sentence land inside his chest like a small, warm bird.  
12. Over the following weeks, they met every evening.  
13. Elise brought books on medieval fortification; Daniel brought pastries from the Polish bakery.  
14. They read aloud to each other, voices mingling with the wind that rattled the turret’s louvers.  
15. One night, she traced the mortar lines with her fingertip and said, “These gaps are where stories leak out.”  
16. Daniel wanted to tell her that he was falling in love, but the words felt too heavy for the narrow roof.  
17. Instead, he asked, “Why turrets?”  
18. Elise sat cross-legged, cradling her tea.  
19. “When I was eight, my father renovated our attic into a little round room,” she began.  
20. “It had one window facing the sea, and I would sit there during storms, feeling safe inside the circle.”  
21. “After he died, that room was sealed up.”  
22. “I think I’ve been looking for that feeling ever since.”  
23. Daniel’s throat tightened.  
24. He reached out and brushed a fleck of dried leaf from her sleeve.  
25. She looked at his hand, then at his face, and smiled without speaking.  
26. Snow came early that year, frosting the turret like icing on a wedding cake.  
27. They built a tiny snow battlement along the parapet, complete with flags made of coffee-stirrer sticks.  
28. Elise laughed when Daniel’s flag fell and speared his boot.  
29. Their mittened hands touched while retrieving it.  
30. Neither pulled away.
