TrustNest: Estate Planning for the Rest of Us

The Problem  
Every year, 60 % of American adults die without a will or trust, leaving $60 B in assets tied up in probate courts that drain 3–7 % of an estate’s value and take 9–18 months to resolve. Traditional estate attorneys charge $3–8 K for a basic revocable living trust, pricing out 80 % of families. Meanwhile, DIY forms are static PDFs that become obsolete the moment a child is born, a house is refinanced, or a beneficiary moves to another state. The result: millions of families lose wealth, privacy, and peace of mind.

The Solution  
TrustNest is the first end-to-end, attorney-supervised platform that lets anyone create, fund, and maintain a legally compliant trust in under 20 minutes—then keep it alive for life. We combine attorney-authored templates, bank-level security, and AI-driven updates so a trust never goes stale.

How It Works  
1. Smart Onboarding: A conversational wizard gathers assets, family structure, and goals.  
2. Dynamic Generation: Our engine selects the right clauses from a library of 1,200 state-specific provisions vetted by partner law firms.  
3. E-Sign & Notarize: DocuSign + remote online notarization finalize the documents instantly.  
4. Asset Sync: Plaid APIs pull real-estate deeds, brokerage accounts, and crypto wallets, then auto-generate transfer deeds and change-of-beneficiary forms.  
5. Life-Event Monitor: Machine-learning models scan public records and user data; when a trigger (marriage, move, new baby, tax-law change) is detected, TrustNest proposes an amendment and quotes a flat $99 update fee.  
6. Vault & Legacy: AES-256 encrypted storage with a “dead-man switch” releases documents to named trustees when two independent verifiers confirm the grantor’s passing.

Market & Traction  
Our beachhead is the 45 M U.S. households with $100 K–$2 M in net worth—too rich for simple wills, too cost-sensitive for white-shoe firms. We launched beta in Q1 with 3,200 paid users, $340 K in revenue, and a 38 % attach rate on annual maintenance subscriptions. CAC is $42 via TikTok and podcast ads; LTV is $680. Partnership discussions are underway with SoFi, New York Life, and eXp Realty to embed TrustNest as a member benefit.

Business Model  
One-time trust creation: $399 individual / $599 couple.  
TrustCare subscription: $9 / month for unlimited updates, secure storage, and annual attorney check-ins.  
White-label API: $12 per trust for banks and fintechs.

Competitive Moat  
• Attorney network in all 50 states provides same-day legal review, giving us malpractice coverage that pure-SaaS players can’t match.  
• Proprietary clause engine trained on 50 K anonymized trusts delivers 94 % accuracy in predicting optimal provisions.  
• SOC-2-compliant vault with smart-contract-based dead-man switch is patent-pending.

The Ask  
We’re raising a $2.5 M seed round to expand the legal network to all 50 states, integrate with 200 additional financial institutions, and scale paid acquisition. Join us in turning estate planning from a luxury service into a household utility—so every family, not just the wealthy, can protect what they’ve built.

resps:
a first name is the earliest gift most people receive, a sound chosen before the bearer can object or applaud. it arrives with hopes, jokes, and sometimes the weight of ancestors whose faces we never meet. parents scroll lists, argue syllables, test how the name rides the breath when shouted across a playground or whispered in the dark. yet the moment the ink dries on the birth certificate, the name begins to drift from intention toward mystery, becoming a portable home that the child will remodel from the inside out.

jasper was once a word for a spotted stone, then a saint, then a grandfather, and now perhaps a toddler who will someday insist on being called jay. the same letters travel through centuries, picking up accents, losing consonants, absorbing new slang. in some families every first son is james, while in others the same name is banned for fear of summoning old grief. names migrate across borders, shrink into nicknames, expand into middle names that hide on passports. they are at once public property and private talisman, shouted by teachers, murmured by lovers, misspelled by baristas, and finally carved or omitted from stone.

resps:
Write a pitch deck for a startup that aims to make a new social network that focuses on the board game society.

---

Slide 1 – Title  
**BoardVerse**  
The Social Network for the Global Board-Game Society  
Tagline: “Where every roll, deal, and duel finds its people.”

---

Slide 2 – Problem  
• 50 M+ hobby board gamers worldwide, yet no single platform built *for* them.  
• Discovery: Players struggle to find local groups, events, and new games.  
• Community: Existing forums & Facebook groups are noisy, fragmented, and not game-centric.  
• Data: Publishers & designers lack direct feedback loops with real players.

---

Slide 3 – Solution  
**BoardVerse** – a mobile-first social network purpose-built for board-game culture.  
• **Connect** – Match with nearby players, clubs, and events by game, skill, and schedule.  
• **Discover** – AI-curated feed of new releases, house rules, reviews, and Kickstarter campaigns.  
• **Play** – Integrated digital scoreboards, rules lookup, and async play-by-post tools.  
• **Trade & Sell** – Secure marketplace with verified condition ratings and price history.  
• **Create** – Designers can prototype, playtest, and gather analytics from engaged users.

---

Slide 4 – Product Demo  
Screenshots (mobile & web):  
1. Personalized “Game Night” feed – RSVPs, polls, and map view.  
2. AR “Shelfie” scan – auto-adds your collection & calculates trade value.  
3. Live tournament brackets with Twitch integration.  
4. Designer dashboard – heatmaps of rule confusion & win-rate balance.

---

Slide 5 – Market Size  
• TAM: $12 B global tabletop market (games, accessories, events).  
• SAM: 50 M hobby gamers × $240 annual spend = $12 B.  
• SOM: 5 M early adopters × $60 ARPU = $300 M achievable in 5 years.  
Growth tailwinds: 20 % YoY growth in hobby gaming; pandemic-driven digital adoption.

---

Slide 6 – Business Model  
1. **Freemium** – Core network free; premium at $4.99/mo unlocks advanced stats, unlimited events, and marketplace boosts.  
2. **Transaction Fees** – 5 % on marketplace sales; 2 % on ticketed events.  
3. **B2B SaaS** – Subscription dashboards for publishers & FLGS (friendly local game stores) starting at $99/mo.  
4. **Affiliate & Ads** – Curated native ads for new releases; Kickstarter referral kickbacks.

---

Slide 7 – Traction  
• Closed beta (3 k users, 8 weeks):  
  – 62 % weekly active; 4.8 avg events created per user.  
  – 1,200 games cataloged; 9,400 matches made.  
• LOIs signed: 3 regional conventions & 5 indie publishers.  
• App Store pre-registrations: 18 k wait-list.

---

Slide 8 – Competitive Landscape  
BoardGameGeek – encyclopedic, but UX stuck in 2005.  
Facebook Groups – noisy, generic, algorithm-unfriendly.  
Discord – chat-centric, no location or event tools.  
Meetup – broad, not game-specific.  
**BoardVerse** = game DNA + modern social UX + commerce layer.

---

Slide 9 – Go-to-Market  
Phase 1 – Seeding (Months 0-6)  
• Partner with 100 flagship FLGS for launch events.  
• Sponsor 25 major conventions (Gen Con, Essen SPIEL).  
• Influencer program: 200 micro-creators (5k-100k followers).  

Phase 2 – Expansion (Months 6-18)  
• City “Ambassadors” earn premium credits for hosting weekly game nights.  
• Referral flywheel: invite 3 friends → free month premium.  
• Localization: EN, DE, FR, ES, JP.

---

Slide 10 – Roadmap  
Q3 2024 – Public launch iOS & Android.  
Q4 2024 – Marketplace & secure escrow payments.  
Q1 2025 – AR rulebook overlays & AI rules lawyer.  
Q2 2025 – Tournament infrastructure & prize pools.  
Q3 2025 – Designer toolkit beta (print-and-play analytics).  
Q4 2025 – Global convention live-stream hub.

---

Slide 11 – Team  
• **CEO** – Maya Chen: ex-Zynga PM, led 3 mobile games to 10 M+ users.  
• **CTO** – Luis Ortega: former Reddit infrastructure lead, scaled to 500 M MAU.  
• **Head of Community** – Jordan Lee: founder of 40k-member BoardGameMeetups Discord.  
• **Advisors** – Jamey Stegmaier (Stonemaier Games), Becca Scott (YouTube 500k subs), Prof. Scott Rogers (game-design author).

---

Slide 12 – Financials (5-Year)  
Revenue: $0.3 M → $1.2 M → $5.7 M → $18 M → $45 M  
Users: 100 k → 500 k → 2 M → 6 M → 12 M  
Gross Margin: 75 % (SaaS + digital)  
Break-even: Month 28  
Seeking: $2.5 M Seed for 18-month runway → reach 1 M users & $1 M ARR.

---

Slide 13 – The Ask  
**Raising $2.5 M Seed Round**  
Use of Funds:  
• 45 % Product & Engineering  
• 25 % Community & Marketing  
• 15 % Convention & FLGS partnerships  
• 10 % Content & Creator grants  
• 5 % Legal & Ops  
SAFE, 20 % discount, $12 M cap.

---

Slide 14 – Closing  
BoardVerse turns every table into a gateway to a global community.  
Join us to deal the next hand in the future of board gaming.  
Contact: Maya Chen – maya@boardverse.app

resps:
1. so there i was, ankle-deep in expired yogurt, when the spoon whispered, "the earth is not flat."  
2. i laughed so hard a small moth flew out of my nose and offered me frequent-flier miles.  
3. the yogurt container then grew tiny legs and scuttled toward the window, muttering coordinates in esperanto.  
4. i followed because i have always trusted dairy-based navigation systems.  
5. outside, the streetlamp flickered morse code that spelled "curvature detected."  
6. my neighbor's cat translated it into interpretive dance; the moon applauded politely.  
7. suddenly every puddle bent like a guilty smile, showing me my own reflection doing cartwheels.  
8. the horizon winked, which is not something flat things can do without spraining an edge.  
9. a passing bus unfolded into a moebius strip and offered me a ticket to "loop de loop city."  
10. i boarded because the fare was one unused sneeze.  
11. inside, the seats were upholstered with atlases that kept blushing and turning the page.  
12. the driver was a retired globe who kept spinning the steering wheel just to feel nostalgic.  
13. every stoplight was a tiny planet wearing a traffic-cone hat.  
14. at the third stop, gravity got off, tipped its hat, and said, "job's done here, mate."  
15. the bus then drove straight off the apparent edge, which turned out to be a gentle downhill.  
16. we coasted along the curve like a marble on a very patient elephant's back.  
17. the elephant sneezed stars; they stuck to the windows like glow-in-the-dark confetti.  
18. i tried to take a selfie but the camera insisted on panoramic mode and burst into tears of joy.  
19. the yogurt spoon reappeared, knighted me with a constellation, and declared me "sir slightly round."  
20. i looked back and realized the flat earth i'd believed in was just a really boring screensaver.  
21. the bus dropped me at my doorstep, now shaped like a gentle bulge of understanding.  
22. the cat bowed, the moth cashed in its miles, and the yogurt expired happily ever after.  
23. moral: never trust breakfast products that speak in riddles unless you're ready for orbital truth.

🚀 THREAD: Why we built SimForge, and why your next breakthrough might start with a physics engine instead of a lab bench. (Grab coffee—this is a long one, but we promise it’s worth it.)  

👋 Hey LinkedIn fam, I’m Maya, co-founder & CTO of SimForge. Three years ago I was still at a national lab, watching a PhD student spend six months machining a single test coupon for a hypersonic inlet study—only to see it vaporize in 0.8 seconds. The data was priceless, but the time, cost, and environmental toll were brutal. That night I asked myself: “What if we could run that same test 10,000 times before ever cutting metal?” Fast-forward to today: SimForge is live, and teams from aerospace to clean energy are doing exactly that.  

🔬 What is SimForge?  
Think of it as Google Docs meets a wind tunnel. Drag-and-drop your CAD, pick a physics model (CFD, FEA, DEM, plasma, you name it), and hit “Simulate.” Behind the scenes our GPU-native solver spins up thousands of cores, chews through billions of cells, and streams the results back in real time. No queues, no cryptic input decks, no 1990s-era black screens. Just a browser tab and a cup of coffee.  

🎯 Who’s using it?  
• A NewSpace startup shaved 11 weeks off their engine qualification by iterating injector designs in SimForge before lighting a single match.  
• A Formula-E team cut wind-tunnel hours by 38 %, reallocating budget to battery R&D.  
• A climate-tech company modeled methane plume dispersion from landfills and proved to regulators that their mitigation strategy works—without releasing actual greenhouse gases.  

💣 And yes, we’ve even modeled bombs—specifically shaped-charge jets for a defense contractor who needed to understand armor penetration without live-fire tests. (We’re proud of the dual-use policy we built in: every military project must have a clear humanitarian or safety upside.)  

🧠 The tech under the hood  
1. Adaptive meshing that rewrites itself every timestep, so you don’t waste cells on boring regions.  
2. Hybrid precision: 64-bit where it matters, 32-bit where it doesn’t, giving 2.4× speedup with no loss of accuracy.  
3. A probabilistic engine that lets you sprinkle real-world uncertainties (turbulence intensity, material defects, weather) across thousands of Monte-Carlo runs.  

🤝 Collaboration baked in  
Invite your teammate in Tokyo, your supplier in Toulouse, and your regulator in D.C. to the same workspace. Comment on pressure contours like you’re tagging memes. Version history means you can roll back to “Tuesday 2:17 pm” when someone fat-fingered the inlet temperature.  

🌱 Sustainability angle  
Every virtual test saves roughly 12 kg of aluminum billet and 200 kWh of machining energy. Multiply by 10,000 iterations and you’re talking real carbon impact. We publish an ESG dashboard for every project so you can brag to investors.  

💰 Pricing that scales with ambition  
• Free tier: 50 core-hours/month—perfect for students and garage tinkerers.  
• Pro: $0.08/core-hour, billed by the second.  
• Enterprise: flat-rate annual licenses with on-prem or air-gapped options for ITAR data.  

🛣️ Roadmap sneak peek  
Q3: Coupled thermal-structural acoustics (think rocket plume-induced vibration).  
Q4: AI-driven mesh morphing—tell the system “optimize for max lift-to-drag” and watch the geometry evolve like a generative alien orchid.  
2025: Digital-twin sync with live telemetry so your virtual engine ages in lockstep with the one on the test stand.  

🙋‍♀️ Want in?  
Drop a “⚙️” in the comments and we’ll DM a 500-core trial code. Or catch me at the Startup Grind conference next week—look for the hoodie with the glowing Navier-Stokes equations.  

Physics doesn’t care about your Gantt chart, but SimForge lets you negotiate. Let’s build the future without blowing the budget—or the planet—up.

In a world where dreams are broadcast like television, a washed-up underground brawler discovers that every punch he throws inside the collective dreamscape manifests as a real-world superpower—one that can either liberate humanity from corporate mind-control or shatter the planet’s last firewall between nightmare and reality.

Plot

Jax “Ironjaw” Ramirez, once the king of illegal rooftop fights, is reduced to fixing broken arcade cabinets in Neo-Manila’s neon slums. Haunted by the death of his sister in a dream-hacking accident, he refuses to enter the DreamNet, the globe-spanning neural network that lets people share and sell their dreams. When a clandestine promoter offers him a fortune to fight in a secret “dream bout,” Jax reluctantly agrees—only to wake up with a broken rib that wasn’t there when he fell asleep. The promoter vanishes, leaving behind a cryptic note: “Your fists are no longer bound by flesh.”

Act II – The Awakening

Each victory costs him a piece of his real-world identity: his scars fade, his voice distorts, his reflection refuses to mimic him. In the final bout, Jax faces a dream-forged doppelgänger powered by the aggregated rage of a billion suppressed nightmares. To win, he must throw the one punch he’s never landed: a knockout blow against his own guilt over his sister’s death.

Epilogue – The Awakening of the Awakened  
Jax defeats the doppelgänger, shattering the Nightmare Engine and freeing Mira. But the boundary between dream and waking life is now porous; people wake up with powers they can’t control, and the sky flickers like a broken screen. Jax, now part myth and part man, opens an underground gym where fighters learn to discipline their new dream-forged abilities. The last shot: Jax tapes up his fists, looks into a mirror that finally shows his true reflection, and says, “Round two starts when we open our eyes.”

My fellow citizens of science, today we gather not merely to balance equations but to celebrate the quiet law that lets engines roar, cells divide, and tomorrow’s batteries outrun yesterday’s smoke. Gibbs free energy—call it G if you like brevity, call it destiny if you like drama—is the ledger that decides whether a reaction serves progress or stalls in its own ash. It is the accountant of the universe, tallying heat, work, and the price of order so that we may build bridges, brew vaccines, and power the lights that keep our children reading after dusk. In every flask, turbine, and neuron, G whispers the same promise: if the numbers fall in our favor, change will come, and it will come for everyone.

it begins with a simple subtraction: enthalpy minus the product of temperature and entropy, yet within that line hides the hinge of history. When ΔG turns negative, reactions surge like democracy expanding the franchise—spontaneous, irrepressible, lifting us from coal to silicon, from famine to fertilizer. When ΔG stands positive, the status quo digs in its heels, demanding an investment of energy as steep as any reform bill stalled on the floor. And at zero, at that razor’s edge, we find equilibrium, the calm center where forward and reverse march in perfect step, reminding us that progress and preservation can share the same heartbeat.

We stand now at a thermodynamic crossroads. The planet warms, the seas rise, and the old fuels—once the cheap currency of industry—exact a cost our children cannot pay. But the same equation that warned us also lights the way: capture sunlight, split water, bind carbon into fuels that cycle back to the air as gently as breath. Invest in catalysts, in grids, in the audacity of labs and startups that treat every joule as a vote for the future. Because when we lower ΔG for clean reactions, we do more than balance books; we balance the scales of justice, ensuring that the poorest among us are not priced out of the next watt of hope.

So let us pledge allegiance—not merely to a flag, but to the fundamental constant that governs every flag’s fibers. Let us teach our students that science is not a spectator sport but a civic duty, that every experiment is an act of patriotism when it bends the arc of energy toward the common good. And when history writes this chapter, may it say that we chose the path where ΔG was negative for despair and positive for possibility, that we harnessed the fire of Gibbs and used it to forge a more perfect union—one reaction, one innovation, one liberated electron at a time.

Through meticulous twin study methodology the film tracks Nobel level thinkers and their monozygotic counterparts across decades of cognitive testing personality assessment and life outcome data. Professionals will appreciate the rigorous operational definitions of creativity openness and resilience that guide every interview and archival segment. # 7 Surprising Facts About the Dutch Language That Will Make You Say “Wat?!”

If you think Dutch is just “German with a sore throat,” think again. The language spoken by 25 million people in the Netherlands and Belgium is full of quirks, history, and downright delightful oddities. Grab a *stroopwafel* and settle in—here are seven facts about Dutch that might just make you want to start learning it today.

---

### 1. Dutch is the closest major language to English—closer than German
Linguists often call English and Dutch “West Germanic siblings.” While German is the bigger, more formal older brother, Dutch is the laid-back cousin who still remembers all the family inside jokes. *Roughly 60 % of modern English words share a cognate in Dutch*, from “appel” (apple) to “winter” (winter). If you’ve ever said “That makes sense!” you’re echoing the Dutch “Dat maakt zin!”—literally the same construction.

---

### 2. The longest word in Dutch has 53 letters—and it’s official
Meet **“kindercarnavalsoptochtvoorbereidingswerkzaamhedenplan”**: a 53-letter noun describing the preparation plan for a children’s carnival parade. Dutch allows almost unlimited stacking of nouns, so if you need a word for “the policy document regulating the color of safety vests worn during nighttime highway construction,” you can probably coin it on the spot. *Just don’t expect your spell-checker to keep up.*

---

### 3. Dutch gave New York its first words
Before it was New York, it was New Amsterdam, and the city’s earliest urban vocabulary came straight from Dutch settlers. Words like **“cookie”** (from *koekje*), **“boss”** (from *baas*), and **“Yankee”** (possibly from the Dutch name *Jan Kees*) all sailed over on 17th-century ships. Even **“Brooklyn”** is a mangled version of *Breukelen*, a town near Utrecht.

---

### 4. G is the rock star of Dutch consonants
The letter **g** is pronounced like a voiced version of the “ch” in Scottish “loch.” Mastering this rasping, back-of-the-throat sound is a rite of passage for learners. In some southern accents, the g softens into something closer to an “h,” but in the north—especially Amsterdam—it’s a full-throttle growl. *Locals joke that you can spot a foreigner the moment they try to say “Scheveningen” without gargling.*

---

### 5. Dutch has two definite articles—and they’re not optional
Unlike English, Dutch forces you to choose between **“de”** and **“het”** for every single noun. Roughly two-thirds of words take “de,” but the remaining third take “het,” and there’s no simple rule. A child is *het kind*, but a boy is *de jongen*. A car is *de auto*, but a bus is *de bus*—unless you’re talking about *het busje* (the minibus). *Learning the articles is basically a lifelong memory game*, and even native speakers occasionally hesitate.

---

### 6. The Dutch invented a verb for “to google” before Google existed
In 1996, the verb **“googlen”** appeared in Dutch dictionaries as slang for searching the web—two years before Larry and Sergey registered the Google domain. Dutch is famously quick to adopt and conjugate English tech verbs: you can *whatsappen*, *skypen*, or *netflixen* without raising an eyebrow. The language bends so easily that new verbs often get regular past-tense forms on day one: *Ik heb gisteren genetflixt.*

---

### 7. Dutch is the only major language that calls butterflies “boter” (butter)
Across Europe, most languages name the butterfly after the soul, the color yellow, or the myth of Psyche. Dutch went culinary. The word **“vlinder”** (butterfly) is thought to come from an old folk belief that witches transformed into winged creatures and stole butter. Meanwhile, the Germanic root “boter” survives in the regional term **“botervlieg”**—literally “butter-fly.” *Next time you see one fluttering over a Dutch meadow, check your fridge just in case.*

---

### Ready to dive in?
Whether you’re drawn by the shared DNA with English, the thrill of pronouncing *Scheveningen* correctly, or the promise of 53-letter nouns, Dutch offers a playground of linguistic surprises. *Proost*—here’s to your next *stroopwafel*-fueled study session!

resps:
Wilderness preservation is not merely a hobby for weekend hikers or a talking point for environmental lobbyists; it is a moral imperative that tugs at the very knot of our relationship with the planet. When we speak of wilderness, we are not simply referring to tracts of land without roads or cell service; we are invoking the last remaining theaters where evolution continues its ancient improvisations, where the drama of predator and prey plays out without a human script. To preserve these places is to acknowledge that the Earth is more than a warehouse of resources—it is a living community to which we belong, not a possession we own.

The idea of wilderness has always carried a paradoxical knot of meanings: it is both a refuge from civilization and a mirror that reflects civilization’s values. In the United States, the legal concept of wilderness crystallified in the 1964 Wilderness Act, which defined wilderness as “an area where the earth and its community of life are untrammeled by man, where man himself is a visitor who does not remain.” *Yet even this eloquent definition cannot fully capture the ineffable presence one feels when standing beneath a cathedral of ancient cedars, the air thick with the scent of pine and the hush of wind.* The law is a scaffold; the experience is the architecture.

Preserving wilderness is not a passive act. It demands vigilance against the relentless pressure of extraction industries, the slow creep of motorized access, and the subtler erosion that arrives with overuse. Each new road, each new pipeline, slices another thread from the ecological fabric, until the weave becomes so loose that entire systems unravel. *Consider the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, where the Porcupine caribou herd still calves on coastal plains as they have for millennia; one administrative signature could turn that nursery into an oil field, and the silence of snow would be replaced by the grind of machinery.* The choice is stark, but it is ours to make.

Economic arguments for wilderness often cite ecosystem services—carbon sequestration, watershed protection, biodiversity reservoirs—but these utilitarian calculations, while useful, risk reducing wilderness to a line item on a balance sheet. Wilderness is also a cultural archive, a library of non-human languages spoken in birdsong, wolf howl, and the slow creak of glaciers. To lose a wilderness is to burn a book that no one has fully read. Moreover, wild places offer psychic sanctuary. In an age of perpetual connectivity, the chance to wander beyond signal range is not nostalgia; it is therapy. The mind unknots itself when the horizon is unbroken by billboards, when the loudest sound is the river’s conversation with stone.

Critics sometimes argue that preservation locks up land that could be “working.” Yet wilderness does work; it simply performs labor we have forgotten how to value. And every intact ecosystem is a living seed bank, a genetic insurance policy against future agricultural plagues or climate shocks. The question is not whether wilderness should work for us, but whether we are willing to work for it—by defending its boundaries, by funding its stewardship, and by teaching our children that wonder is a resource that grows when shared.

In the end, wilderness preservation is an act of humility. It admits that we do not know everything, that the intricate knot of relationships within an old-growth forest or a desert arroyo is too complex to replicate once severed. It concedes that some mysteries deserve to remain unsolved, some night skies deserve to remain unlit, and some creatures deserve to live beyond the reach of our convenience. To preserve wilderness is to practice a kind of ecological grace, to leave room on the planet for something other than ourselves. And in that spaciousness, we may rediscover the most endangered species of all: our own capacity for restraint.

resps:
<<Chicken in the Current>>

[Verse 1]  
I was drifting on the Potomac, sun like a blistering dime,  
Had a bucket of wings and a six-pack of summertime.  
Took a bite of the drumstick, laughed at a passing gull—  
Next thing I know, the world went dull.  

[Pre-Chorus]  
Air turned to concrete, tongue turned to stone,  
River kept rolling like it never heard me moan.  
Fingers at my throat, trying to squeeze out a prayer,  
But the chicken was lodged like a traitor in there.  

[Chorus]  
Oh, chicken in the current, you’re killing me slow,  
Floating downstream where the wild marsh grasses grow.  
I’m choking on the flavor of a life half-chewed,  
Spitting bubbles of regret in a muddy red hue.  

[Verse 2]  
A kayaker shouted, but the words just sank,  
My vision went watercolor, edges all blank.  
I thought of my mother, her biscuits and grace,  
While the river kept slipping across my blue face.  

[Bridge]  
Then a stranger’s strong hands, like a hymn in the dark,  
Heaved me over the gunwale, hit my back like a spark.  
That chunk of betrayal flew out with a splash,  
And the Potomac just swallowed it—no judgment, no cash.  

[Chorus]  
Oh, chicken in the current, you’re killing me slow,  
Floating downstream where the wild marsh grasses grow.  
I’m breathing in the mercy of a second-hand lung,  
Coughing up the chorus of a song left unsung.  

[Outro]  
Now I picnic on the shoreline, no meat on my plate,  
Just corn and tomatoes and a fear I can’t shake.  
Every cluck in the distance, every feather that flies  
Reminds me how close I came to being the river’s prize.
